title: 'We Need to Rethink': Muzumdar Demands Strategic Overhaul as India Women's T20 World Cup Failures Become a Pattern
excerpt: Back-to-back group-stage exits, bowling frailties, and a captaincy question mark — coach Amol Muzumdar and experts map out what must change
body:
India's women's cricket team walked off Lord's on Sunday carrying a weight far heavier than one loss. Their six-wicket defeat to Australia did not just end their ICC Women's T20 World Cup 2026 campaign — it confirmed a troubling pattern. For the second consecutive edition, India have been eliminated in the group stage, unable to beat the teams that matter most when it matters most.

Head coach Amol Muzumdar did not sugarcoat the situation. Speaking to the media after the match, the former domestic batting great called for a fundamental rethink of India's T20 approach.

"I think we really need to work on our bowling and fielding. We also need to be a little more aggressive with the bat. Maybe we could have had an extra 15-20 runs as a cushion," Muzumdar said. "We need to really go back and think how we're going to approach the T20 game."

## The Numbers Tell a Familiar Story

India's tournament trajectory was a near-exact repeat of their 2024 campaign in Sharjah. In both editions, the Women in Blue dispatched weaker opposition — this time Pakistan, the Netherlands, and Bangladesh — but crumbled against the top sides. Losses to South Africa in Manchester and Australia at Lord's left them watching the knockout rounds from the sidelines.

Against Australia, India's batters actually showed intent. Captain Harmanpreet Kaur played a blistering knock of 56 off 27 balls, openers Smriti Mandhana and Shafali Verma put on a 66-run stand, and the total of 170 for 4 was India's highest against Australia in T20 World Cup history. But the bowling and fielding let them down completely.



> **"Muzumdar, for his part, gave a "short and sweet" answer: yes, he wants her to continue."**


Ellyse Perry (56 off 38) and Ashleigh Gardner (53 off 29) shared a decisive 100-run partnership for the fourth wicket, and Australia chased down the target with five balls to spare. India's top-ranked T20I bowler Sree Charani bowled a costly no-ball at a critical juncture, while a misfield from Kranti Gaud gifted four runs. Small margins, but in knockout cricket, they are everything.

## Harmanpreet's Future: Backed but Uncertain

With six T20 World Cups as captain and a record that peaks at the 2020 final before declining through successive early exits, the question of Harmanpreet Kaur's leadership was inevitable. Muzumdar, for his part, gave a "short and sweet" answer: yes, he wants her to continue. But he pointedly noted that the decision "is up to the selectors."


![World Cup — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fb/Kitzbuehel_slalom_ganslernhang_2010.jpg)


Cricket experts have largely backed the 37-year-old, though not without caveats. Former India captain Anjum Chopra, speaking on JioStar, said she doesn't think "any other player is ready for captaincy at this point" but flagged a long list of tactical issues — from unclear batting positions to the delayed promotion of power-hitter Richa Ghosh, who should have been sent in earlier to capitalise on the death overs.

## Fitness, Fearlessness, and the WPL Disconnect

Commentator Aakash Chopra zeroed in on an issue that goes beyond tactics: fitness. "If you want to compete against Australia, South Africa and New Zealand in the shortest format, you'll have to be a lot fitter," he said. "Your fielding, how well you cover the ground, and how far you can hit the ball matter a lot more."

Anjum Chopra raised a deeper structural concern. Indian players show fearless, attacking cricket in the Women's Premier League, but "as soon as they come back to the Indian team, they go into their shell again." The gap between franchise freedom and international pressure remains a puzzle India's coaching staff have yet to solve.

Muzumdar himself acknowledged the bowling unit's inexperience, asking for patience. "Give us 18 months and this bowling attack will be a very different one," he said. The injury to experienced spinner Sneh Rana and the late inclusion of seamer Renuka Singh Thakur further disrupted what was already a developing bowling lineup.

## The Diaspora Watches — and Waits

For the Indian diaspora in the United Kingdom, this was supposed to be a celebration. The 2025 ODI World Cup champions arriving at Lord's — the home of cricket — to play in front of a crowd that included thousands of NRI fans who had snapped up tickets months in advance. Instead, they witnessed the same script they have seen before: competitive totals, fragile bowling, and a heartbreaking exit.

The sting is sharper because the next T20 World Cup is two years away in 2028, and the window for this generation of players is closing. The road back begins almost immediately — India tour England for five T20Is and three ODIs starting July 1, with the series opener at Headingley. It is a chance for Muzumdar to begin implementing the very changes he has called for, under the watchful eyes of a diaspora that has invested not just money in tickets but genuine emotion in this team's dream of a maiden T20 World Cup title.

The talent is there. The intent, as Muzumdar insists, is there. What has been missing — ruthlessness under pressure, bowling consistency, elite fielding, and a T20 identity distinct from their ODI excellence — will define whether the next two years look different from the last four.

*Sources: ICC, Reuters, SportsTak, Bhaskar English, RevSportz*
